Photograph: Michael Sohn/Reuters View image in fullscreen The BND headquarters in Berlin will gain new powers to confront threats from state actors such as Russia and China, using the help of AI. Photograph: Michael Sohn/Reuters Germany Germany approves lifting curbs on spy agencies in security ‘revolution’ Reforms comply with wishlist of intelligence services which say Germany lags behind allies and enemies Deborah Cole in Berlin Wed 12 Aug 2026 06.43 EDT First published on Wed 12 Aug 2026 06.42 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The German government has approved a draft law aimed at lifting many of the restraints on its spy agencies imposed during the postwar period as the country reels from two attacks in a month that have exposed serious security gaps. The controversial changes, which must still pass parliament, largely comply with a wishlist pulled together by the foreign and domestic intelligence services, which have long complained Germany lags behind its allies and enemies. “We are turning our intelligence services into genuine secret services,” the interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, told Bild newspaper, which called it a security “revolution” and “historic”. He said: “It is high time we positioned ourselves to be competitive and on an equal footing with our partner services around the world. This requires operational capabilities and active powers to tackle modern state terrorism and extremist groups more effectively.” A deadly car ramming in late July at Berlin’s huge annual Pride parade by a German-born Islamist known to the authorities was followed by the discovery last week of a drone laden with explosives near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig airport, a key defence transport hub. Friedrich Merz ’s unpopular centre-right, centre-left coalition government is under pressure to demonstrate it can modernise to keep its citizens safe, while preserving rights and principles laid out in Germany’s Basic Law . View image in fullscreen The federal minister of the interior, Alexander Dobrindt, called the approval of the draft laws ‘historic’. Photograph: dts News Agency Germany/Shutterstock The intelligence services reform plans have been in the offing for months and were repeatedly fine-tuned before being presented to the cabinet on Wednesday. The federal foreign intelligence service (BND), which turned 70 this year and is run by a former ambassador to Ukraine, Martin Jäger, will gain new powers to confront emerging threats from state actors such as Russia and China with fewer impediments, and with the help of AI. German authorities say the threat level has soared since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 as agents linked to Moscow have allegedly carried out repeated sabotage, spying and hacker attacks against critical infrastructure and military equipment manufacturers. Jäger said Germany must be able to show adversaries “that we’re in a position to do similar things so the other side also feels the pain”. The BND has until now overwhelmingly had a defensive position, making it largely a repository for information with few operational powers. According to the draft law’s more than 700-page text, German spies will have permission to manipulate or delete data known as “hack-back” cyber-attacks. Other options include, altering instructions on how to build weapons or rendering arms harmless during production. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion US intelligence ‘believes Russia was behind Leipzig airport drone bomb’ Read more Digital payments to low-level “disposable” agents , employed on a one-off basis by foreign governments, could be blocked to thwart attacks. The use of force by intelligence personnel abroad will remain forbidden – keeping it far out of the league of the CIA, the Mossad in Israel or the DGSE in France. But agents will be able to carry weapons for self-defence more often without explicit permission. The law, which the government hopes will be in place by 1 January 2027, would loosen rules around data protection, widely mocked as exaggerated and self-defeating . The BND and the domestic security watchdog, the Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV), will be unshackled to collect, store and analyse more information for longer with the help of AI. It will also be easier to gain permission for online searches and home surveillance against criminal suspects. Germany will also beef up oversight of the BND and the BfV by an independent board, in addition to powers already granted to parliament’s intelligence control committee. Although reforms were widely seen as necessary and overdue, some politicians warned of overreach. The federal commissioner for data protection, Louisa Specht-Riemenschneider, said her office would be stripped of oversight powers over the BND and criticised the expanded access to CCTV footage in public spaces in Germany and abroad. Konstantin von Notz, the opposition Green party’s spokesperson on intelligence oversight, called the changes “urgently needed” and said he backed “stronger powers” for the BND. But he said the draft law “overshoots the mark”. He was particularly critical of the powers granted to the BfV, which he said were “difficult to reconcile” with the principle of separation between the powers of the intelligence services and the police – a lesson drawn from the darkest chapters of German history. The legislation could face court challenges mounted by its critics. Faced with rising geopolitical uncertainty and doubts about the role of the US as guarantor of the country’s security, Germany is also in a major rearmament drive. Merz took office last year pledging to turn Germany’s armed forces, or Bundeswehr, into “Europe’s strongest conventional army” . https://www.kuow.org/immigration/2026-10.text: On Air Now Playing KUOW FM On Air Now Playing Newscast Immigration Community Voices Network People in Western Washington tell us what's on their minds KUOW's Community Voices Network aims to expand the range of opinions that we hear on KUOW. To broaden the conversation, we're speaking with a diverse pool of people who represent a wide array of political perspectives, cultural backgrounds, and life experiences. 7 Washingtonians share their views on Trump's immigration policy KUOW | By Ruby de Luna , Alex Rochester , Deborah Wang Published October 12, 2026 at 4:18 PM PDT Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Listen • 5:28 The Trump administration's immigration crackdown continues to divide Americans, and polls show declining support for the president’s mass deportation campaign. A recent poll by Fox News found President Donald Trump’s approval rating on immigration now stands at 43%, down five percentage points from last summer. A majority of respondents said immigration enforcement has gone too far. A September poll by Politico found mass deportations are causing wider divisions within Trump’s base. Sponsored Washington state saw a surge of ICE activity this summer, according to KUOW’s recent analysis of ICE datasets obtained by the Deportation Data Project . According to the data, the majority of arrests were of people who had no criminal record. Seven Washington residents shared their thoughts about the current immigration crackdown. Their participation is part of KUOW’s Community Voices Network , a project that asks a diverse group of community members to weigh in on the big issues of the day. Read more about why we are investing in this kind of reporting and how we are recruiting people for the project here . Photo courtesy of Mark Ibay Mark Ibay became a naturalized U.S. citizen in 2025. He said the current ICE enforcements scare him that he carries a passport card with him at all times. Mark Ibay, 25, Parkland, WA “I’ve had relatives who were pulled over; they were questioned for hours on end.” Mark Ibay is a clerk at Western State Hospital. He immigrated from the Philippines to the U.S. in 2019 and became a naturalized citizen in 2025. Even with that status, Ibay says he can’t help but worry. “I carry my passport card with me wherever I go,” Ibay said. “The current enforcement is really scary.” Sponsored He said he understands these efforts are targeted at people with criminal records or those who are here unlawfully, according to the Trump administration. But he said the way it’s carried out seems harsh. Ibay said the administration’s approach and the way Immigration and Customs Enforcement is carrying out detentions and deportations is having a negative impact on immigrant communities. “There are a lot of innocent souls out there who also get caught in the crossfire,” he said. Politically, Ibay considers himself “neutral,” adding that he prefers candidates who will actually do the work and follow up on their plans. He said he’s still trying to learn about his new home and its systems. “We’re here to build community,” Ibay said. “Because you’ve given us the opportunity, we want to give it back.” KUOW Photo/Ruby de Luna Diana McAllister said the Trump administration's arrests and deportations are exactly what she voted for. Diana McAllister, 75, Arlington, WA “It’s one of the things I voted for, was get tough, take a stand, and make it happen.” Sponsored Diana McAllister supports the Trump Administration’s deportation efforts — it’s the policy she voted for. “If they’re not citizens, they don’t have rights in this country. They’ve not paid their dues,” McAllister said. “If they come into this country illegally, they need to go home.” McAllister is founder of the Family Academy, which educates parents on how to homeschool their children. She said she was once a card-carrying Democrat. Her mother was active in the party; dinner at the family table often included party stalwarts like Warren Magnuson, Scoop Jackson, and Mike Lowry. Now she describes herself as ultra-conservative. McAllister’s views changed when she had children and decided to homeschool them. “My ideas, my values changed from ultra-liberal, ‘We need to take care of everybody and give stuff away,’ to ‘No, I want to take care of my own,’” she said. McAllister understands there are industries that rely on immigrants for labor. At one time she tried to help a local business with visa applications for its workers. She found the process burdensome, but she still believes employers need to make the effort to hire people legally. “If you’re coming to work and you’re a farmer and you need workers, and these guys are willing to do the job, then do it,” McAllister said. “Register them so they have a background of having been productive and appropriate. Help them in that way.” Sponsored KUOW Photo/Ruby de Luna Gabriel Dias, a trans woman, moved from Florida to Washington state in 2022. "This is a place that I could be myself and continue to help people who need help," Dias said. Gabriel Dias, 24, Renton, WA “We’re seeing families torn apart.” When Gabriel Dias is not working with special needs students as a paraeducator, they monitor ICE enforcement activities as part of a citizens’ rapid-response team. “We show up to make sure the process is legal and that no one’s rights are being violated,” Dias said. Dias is a trans woman. They started getting involved in local groups monitoring ICE when they lived in Florida in 2021 to begin transitioning. It was a rough place to be trans or to be an organizer, they said. The following year, Dias moved to Washington state. “This is a place that I could be myself and continue to help people who need help,” they said. “It wasn’t safe to help people in Florida and I am [able to safely help people] now.” In an ideal world, Dias said the U.S. would have an immigration system with a legal pathway to citizenship that’s easier for people who are not criminals. For example, the system should have more immigration judges. Sponsored Dias said the recent ICE enforcements have been alarming. They noted that the arrests were originally focused on people with criminal records, but now the goal has shifted to include those without criminal records. “We’re seeing families torn apart,” Dias said. “At what point is it just, ‘We don’t want immigrants anymore.’” Alex Rochester / KUOW Frank Schin outside the Vashon Island King County Library Frank Schin, 82, Vashon Island, WA “It has gone vastly overboard and vastly wrong.” Frank Schin considers himself a social conservative, but also as someone who helps those who can’t make it on their own. He voted for Donald Trump once, in 2016. Schin said for decades, the government has allowed people to cross the borders illegally by looking the other way. He said it’s a good idea to correct that. “If they have the name of an individual that is here in the country illegally, (and) they are wanted for a serious crime — those people should be arrested and they should be sent back to their country,” Schin said. Sponsored But he doesn’t approve of the way the administration is handling the issue and the people it has hired to be enforcers. “I think the people working on that job have to be screened more carefully,” Schin said. “They can’t find people and so they were taking anybody and they weren’t checking the credentials of some of these people.” Schin said he’s not against people coming to the country, especially to fill positions in industries that need them, including health care and agriculture. “We need to get more people in here to help us, but we also need to secure the border,” he said. “So, there’s some tough situations to decide how you do it.” Courtesy of Cheryl Hanson Cheryl Hanson Cheryl Hanson, 57, Renton, WA “The old adage of treating people the way you want to be treated is something that has been infused in me as a child and that really influences the way I think about immigration.” The vast majority of Cheryl Hanson’s career has been recruiting for tech companies and philanthropic organizations. Many of the people she has helped hire were from other countries. Sponsored “Even if we did only hire from U.S. universities… we would have to consider students who were from other countries,” Hanson said. “Because so many of our graduate programs in highly specialized areas cannot find enough students that are U.S. citizens to apply for these positions and pay tuition for our universities.” Hanson said she’s alarmed by how ICE enforcements have been carried out, saying they’re neither humane nor democratic. “I do understand the need for ensuring that we are not allowing people into the country who are terrorists or murderers,” Hanson said. “The reality is that immigrants comprise a much lower percentage of crimes than the overall population.” Hanson said her perspective toward immigrants is shaped in part by her family history. Her grandfather was initially denied entry to the United States after fleeing Poland in the 1920s. But he entered anyway. Hanson believes that had he gone back, he would’ve perished in the Holocaust. “I wouldn’t exist if he hadn’t been allowed into the U.S,” Hanson said. “I’m eternally grateful that he made it here, eventually became a citizen, and built a family and business and contributed to [the] community.” Deborah Wang / KUOW Levi Sweeney poses for a portrait inside his family's print shop Levi Sweeney, 30, Skyway, WA “I keep saying, immigration is not my number one problem, but I've never met an immigrant I didn't like.” Sponsored Levi Sweeney refers to himself as a “dyed-in-the-wool Republican.” He voted for Trump in 2024, although not with much enthusiasm. He calls Trump “the best of a bunch of bad options.” Sweeney currently works as a janitor in his family’s printing business. He is also a writer and self-publishes his novels. He said he believes immigration policy under Trump is “going in the right direction, more or less.” He describes the Biden administration immigration policy as “lax.” He believes “illegal immigrants who are career criminals should absolutely be deported.” But he is more circumspect about people who are in the country without authorization but who “have a clean record, who are just regular guys and gals, who have held down jobs and contributed to their community.” “[They] should of course be given leniency,” he said. But that would mean changing immigration policies to allow for workers to come to the U.S. legally, Sweeney said. Sponsored “I would love it if they could live in this country legally, and could easily migrate here without breaking any laws,” he said. Sweeney doesn’t believe that many people voted for President Trump because he promised to crack down on illegal immigration. He believes most were concerned about bread and butter issues, like the economy, jobs, and housing. In terms of the people who are being arrested on the streets by ICE, he said it's unfortunate. “I'd prefer it didn't have to happen at all, to be frank,” he said. KUOW Photo/Deborah Wang Teacher Leona Oliveros in the office of her home in Federal Way, WA. Leona Oliveros, 33, Federal Way, WA “The movement of people is usually part of a bigger system, bigger injustice that we might not be able to see individually… but it’s there.” As a history teacher, immigration is top of mind for Leona Oliveros. She teaches at Highline College where about a third of the students enrolled are not U.S.-born citizens. Sponsored Oliveros said she makes room for them to talk about their families’ immigration stories to help them see there’s no standard experience. “Some of my students, there can be tension when talking about immigration, legal versus illegal, like, ‘Why would you do it this way, I had to do it the legal way?’” she said. That sentiment resonates within her family, according to Oliveros. Like many of her older family members, her parents came to the U.S. from the Philippines by enlisting in the military; it was a pathway to citizenship. “There’s this assumption that all other undocumented immigration is like jumping the border and the desert and not having the empathy to see that it’s not as simple as that,” she said. Oliveros sees how current ICE enforcements are affecting students on campus. When word gets out about potential ICE sightings or activities around the area, students don’t come to school or they worry about how to get to work. “I hate seeing that kind of anxiety among my student body,” Oliveros said. “What’s the American dream if we’re also making it harder to do?” Tags Immigration Immigration and Customs Enforcement Immigration in the Northwest Trump and the Northwest Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Ruby de Luna Ruby de Luna is a reporter with a focus on food and how it intersects with health, communities, and culture. She has also reported on health care, and immigrant communities.
